correctness.rationale: The frozen iff for two distinct interior fixed points was false as written: two n=2 classes with δ=1/2 and 3/2 at equal weights give H≡1/2 and A=B=0; at r=2 every point is fixed. The repair consistently requires two isolated equilibria and explains the affine and continuum cases. Each active nonlinear class contributes strictly positive curvature throughout the interval; otherwise H is affine. For strict convexity the endpoint slopes characterize the interior minimum, and the line 1/r must be strictly between that minimum and both endpoint values. The +,−,+ drift supplies the two attractors and two repellers. An opposite-slope pair with exponent factors u≤1≤v has a feasible weight ratio exactly when u<v, which holds if either chosen class has size at least three. The repair identifies z(t) as the saddle-node location, not the stable branch itself. The implicit function theorem gives z=κt/c+O(t²) and Taylor expansion gives H_t(0)−H_t(z)=κ²t²/(2c)+O(t³); the product of the two positive H-values gives the inverse-threshold coefficient. Reflection gives the right-end formula with positive right-slope speed. Independent exact expansion of the three-class witness gives A=−11t/12, B=905/2816−19t/12, H₀(0)=31/88 and c=251/704, yielding 20614528/2170899 exactly. The proof covers general parameters; the supplied finite script was inspected, not executed.

value.rationale: The exact weight criterion permits deciding from class parameters whether any mixture, including one with all classes active, can support two attracting outcomes, without sweeping r or solving high-degree equations. The opening width and its coefficient quantify how much parameter room for cooperative bistability is gained on crossing the feasibility boundary. Correcting the continuum case makes this a usable classification of isolated states; generic convexity alone is not the asserted contribution.
